summary: Defines an XML document type that describes the phone book a roaming user needs to find dial-up access points. It specifies the structure and meaning of the entries. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When you travel, you need a list of local numbers to call to get online. This is a standard way to write that list so any program can read it.

subtitle: An XML format for the list of dial-up access points a roaming user needs to get online through another ISP.

tldr.problem: Roaming consortia and their member ISPs need to give users a list of access points and the settings to connect through them, and without a common format each party would build and read the list differently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an XML DTD for the roaming phone book. A phoneBook holds pop elements (points of presence) with a few required items such as address and media, plus optional setup, support and provider information.
tldr.outcome: Phone books can be generated, merged and filtered by many different tools, and IANA can register new elements and attribute values without breaking older documents. Distribution and updating of phone books are out of scope.

today: RFC 3017 is a Proposed Standard (December 2000), and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC leaves phone book distribution and updates to other means and defines only the format.

sections.title: Why a Roaming Phone Book
sections.content:
In roaming, individual ISPs contribute information about their services to a roaming consortium, which assembles a unified phone book for its users. Different groups of users may get different versions, and users may extract subsets, such as only the entries for one country or only access points with wireless connectivity.

The RFC therefore wants a portable, well-formed structure that is easy to generate and post-process. Its goals are a flexible, extensible and robust framework, a standard format that promotes interoperability between ISPs and consortia and lets devices extract configuration data automatically, and a compact structure that can be stored and updated even on small devices.

It explicitly does not try to cover every condition on earth, and it does not define any phone book update or transfer protocol.
sections.eli5: A group of Internet companies shares one big address book of places to dial in. Everyone needs to write that book the same way so any program can read it.

sections.title: Why XML and Typed Values
sections.content:
The RFC chooses XML because it is a standard format for exchanging data and works across media such as paper, CD-ROM and the web. It names three benefits: extensibility, flexibility and integration with directories. Phone books are living documents, so designers need to add new attributes in a well-understood way.

XML DTDs only offer #PCDATA for element content, so the RFC adds four notation declarations for stronger typing: FQDN (fully qualified domain name), IPADR (IP address), B64JPG and B64GIF (Base64-encoded JPEG and GIF images). Elements meant for people to read just use #PCDATA.
sections.eli5: XML is like a set of labeled boxes. A box marked 'phone number' holds a number, and the labels let any program know what is inside.

sections.title: The Container Elements
sections.content:
The phoneBook element is the top container. It has two required attributes, name and version, and holds one or more pop elements. It may also hold setup, support and provider elements, which POPs can reference when several share them. The version is a monotonically increasing integer that should be incremented whenever the phone book changes, so a server can decide what a client needs to catch up.

A pop (point of presence) describes one network access point. Its required items are the address, the media and an entryVersion attribute, again a counter that should increase when the entry changes. The rest is optional: minimum and maximum data rate, properties, tunneling protocols, a dialing script, pricing, city, region and country, and either a local or a referenced setup, support and provider.

The other containers carry the details. setup holds service settings that may differ from provider to provider, such as servers and user name affixes. support holds telephone numbers or mailto URLs for customer support, with an optional language attribute. provider holds general business information such as name, icon, web URL, email addresses and postal details.
sections.eli5: The phone book is a binder. Each page is one place you can dial into, and pages can point to shared sheets about the company and who to call for help.

sections.title: Information Elements
sections.content:
The address element holds the POP's address. For dial-up it contains at least a telephone number string in standard format, and it has a required family attribute, either E164 or X121, plus optional countryCode and areaCode.

The media element lists what the POP supports: viaMODEM, viaISDN, viaATM, viaFR and viaX25. Each is an empty element with an optional type. Modem types run from V21 (300) to V90 (56k), and ISDN types include V110L, X75 and HDLC.

A POP may also declare properties (MPPP, MOBIP, MCRX, MCTX) and tunneling protocols (L2TP, PPTP, L2F, ATMP, AHT, ESPT, IPIP, MIP, GRE).

Setup elements name the DNS server, NNTP, SMTP, POP3 and IMAP servers, WWW, FTP and Winsock proxies, the default gateway, and a userNamePrefix or userNameSuffix. For example, a suffix of @bigco.com turns the base name userA into userA@bigco.com.
sections.eli5: Each page of the binder has blanks to fill in: the phone number, what kind of modem answers, which servers to use, and what to add to your user name.

sections.title: Extending the DTD
sections.content:
The DTD is split into an extensible part with only parameter entity declarations and a fixed part with the detailed structure. IANA maintains the extensible part. New attribute values for the enumerated lists (address families, modem, ISDN, ATM, Frame Relay and X.25 protocols, POP properties and tunneling protocols) are assigned by Specification Required.

New information elements, added by editing the entities mediaTypes, popInformation, setupInformation, supportInformation and providerInformation, need the approval of a Designated Expert, because misuse of the XML content model can break backward compatibility. Any added element must be optional so documents valid under the older DTD stay valid.
sections.eli5: The rules let new blanks be added to the form later, but only as optional ones, so old filled-in forms still count.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Secure distribution of a roaming phone book needs reliable authentication of the issuer and a way to protect the integrity of the information. The DTD itself has no security elements. The RFC assumes security is provided outside this specification, for example by signing the phone book using PGP.
sections.eli5: The format does not lock the binder. If you need to know it is the real one, somebody has to sign it some other way.

data.title: Simplest phone book
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE phoneBook SYSTEM "roamPhoneBook.dtd">
<phoneBook name="minimalExample" version="1">
   <pop entryVersion="1">
      <address family="E164">+1 234 5678901</address>
      <media><viaMODEM/></media>
   </pop>
</phoneBook>
